new.title: A Unified Model for the Gravitational Wave Background and Quasar Luminosity Functions
new.summary: The supermassive black hole mass function (BHMF) is a necessary ingredient in our understanding of how BHs grow and evolve with their host galaxies. Estimations of the BHMF based on observations of local BHs, quasars, and gravitational wave data yield inconsistent results, leading to large uncertainties in, e.g., BH accretion and seeding models. The nanohertz gravitational wave background (GWB) has been a powerful tool to provide constraints on the BHMF across cosmic time. We take posterior BHMFs that describe the GWB and fit them to bolometric quasar luminosity functions (QLF) across $0.2 \leq z \leq 6.2$ to constrain the Eddington ratio distribution function (ERDF). Compared to a fiducial BHMF, based on galaxy and a local black hole mass scaling relation, the BHMFs that match the GWB can reproduce the observed QLFs with lower Eddington fractions and without requiring significant super-Eddington accretion. We use a double power-law form of the ERDF and find that the fits using the GWB-inferred BHMF have systematically lower break-points and marginally steeper slopes in the high-Eddington fraction portion of the function. Furthermore, the best-fit QLFs using the GWB-inferred BHMFs provide better fits to the high-luminosity end of the QLF data than the fiducial model. For both models the ERDF shows significant redshift evolution of the break-point which reaches a maximum around $z \sim 2$. Overall, our prescription can produce realistic QLFs from BHMFs and our GWB-based model is consistent with electromagnetic and gravitational wave data sets.

new.title: Exploring the origin of slow-rotating pulsars: Emission from STARS simulated white dwarfs
new.summary: An increasing number of slow-rotating pulsars and long-period transients have been observed in recent years. The periods of these sources can be significantly longer than typical pulsar sources, ranging from ~ 100 - 1000 s, or even longer. The observed periods and period derivatives predict high magnetic fields, higher than the Schwinger field, when we consider conventional pulsar models of dipole-driven emission from neutron stars. Interestingly, the periods of these sources are consistent with the current observations of white dwarfs (WDs). We explore the possibility of magnetic WDs, simulated using the stellar evolution code STARS, as the origin of some of these unusual pulsar observations. We simulate WDs with enhanced magnetic fields due to accretion after their formation. We also briefly touch on the more exotic possibility of super-Chandrasekhar WDs as the origin for these sources. We find that expanding the parameter space to include the possibility of a WD origin provides an alternate and viable explanation for these unusual observations.

new.title: The (missing) gamma-ray counterparts to EP events
new.summary: While the connection of Fast X-ray Transients (FXTs) detected by Einstein Probe (EP) with Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs) is increasingly compelling, most lack gamma-ray counterparts, leaving their relation to GRBs unclear. We performed a systematic search for gamma-ray counterparts to the 72 transients detected by EP in its first year, using targeted searches in Fermi/GBM and Fermi/LAT data, complemented by SVOM/GRM, SVOM/ECLAIRs, Swift/BAT and Konus-Wind. For the visible events without a gamma-ray counterpart, we derived simultaneous $3\sigma$ flux upper limits in the 10-1000 keV and the 0.1-1 GeV band. We find that 23 events (32%) have a gamma-ray counterpart (seven sub-threshold), while 49 events (68%) have none, despite most being visible. For events with a gamma-ray counterpart, the X-ray flux over the gamma-ray $T_{\rm 90}$ is systematically higher than over the full X-ray duration, with flux ratios $1 \lesssim F_{\rm [10-1000\,keV]}/F_{\rm [0.5-4\,keV]} \lesssim 100$, suggesting that gamma-rays are preferentially detected during the brightest X-ray phases. For events without gamma-ray counterpart, the most stringent Fermi/GBM upper limits imply $E_{\rm peak} \lesssim 30$-100 keV and, for the 14 events with measured redshifts, $L_{\rm iso}\lesssim 10^{48}-9\times10^{51}$ erg/s. If classical GRB correlations hold in this regime, these lower energetics imply lower bulk Lorentz factors ($\Gamma_0 \lesssim 100$), as confirmed in a few cases by afterglow constraints. No significant GeV emission was detected by Fermi/LAT, yielding $1 \lesssim F_{0.1-1\,{\rm GeV}}/F_{0.5-4\,{\rm keV}} \lesssim 10$, placing the first constraints on a potential synchrotron self-Compton component for this new population. Although individual origins remain uncertain, many EP FXTs could be compatible with the GRB population, extending it toward lower $E_{\rm peak}$, luminosities, and bulk Lorentz factors.

new.title: Prior volume effect inflates the gravitational-wave background in pulsar timing arrays
new.summary: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) have found evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background (GWB) whose amplitude exceeds most predictions based on supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). Using NANOGrav 15-year data, we show that a substantial part of this excess arises from a prior volume effect. The GWB amplitude is constrained mainly by the pulsars' auto-correlations, where the GWB is degenerate with each pulsar's intrinsic red noise. By decomposing the GWB posterior, we find that marginalizing over the standard log-uniform red-noise priors introduces a prior volume term that favors a stronger GWB, pulling the inferred amplitude more than $2\sigma$ above the maximum-likelihood estimate. The Hellings-Downs (HD) cross-correlations, which measure the GWB alone, are not strong enough to counter the volume term. The profile likelihood, a cross-correlation-only estimator, and priors that are uniform in power or informed by the pulsar population all avoid or reduce this effect and lower the amplitude into agreement with SMBHBs. The revised priors also yield a steeper GWB spectrum closer to the SMBHB predictions, strengthen the evidence for HD correlations, and weaken the preference for new-physics sources over SMBHBs.

new.title: A Hybrid Neural Network Emulator for M1 Neutrino Reaction Rates in Binary Neutron Star Merger Simulations
new.summary: We present a neural network emulator for the bns_nurates library, which computes neutrino reaction rates used in binary neutron star merger simulations. Following a hybrid strategy, we emulate only the computationally dominant two-dimensional reactions---pair processes, bremsstrahlung, and inelastic neutrino-electron scattering---while evaluating the inexpensive one-dimensional processes still with bns_nurates. We find that the emulator reproduces the opacities to within a few percent across the relevant thermodynamic conditions and accelerates their evaluation by roughly an order of magnitude. When deployed in a global Athenak binary neutron star merger simulation, it recovers the remnant structure, neutrino luminosities, and ejecta composition of a reference run using the full bns_nurates library, at approximately half the overall cost

new.title: Exploring PSR J0901-4046 as an ultra-slowly rotating neutron star versus a white dwarf
new.summary: The source PSR J0901-4046 shows a very long rotational period, of $\approx 75.88$ s. In fact, its long period suggests that it could be a white dwarf. We examine the properties of the source and compare the outcomes under the hypotheses of the source being a highly magnetized white dwarf (B-WD) and neutron star. We find that assuming it to be a B-WD with a surface field $\sim 10^{10}$ G explains many properties, including its storage/rotational energy, explaining luminosity. On the contrary, the neutron star-based idea, particularly if examined under the conventional spin down mechanism, requires an unusually high surface magnetic field $\gtrsim 10^{14}$ G, even exceeding $10^{16}$ G, depending on the obliquity angle and emission mechanism. The source also sits very close to AR Sco, a white dwarf pulsar, in the period and period-derivative plane. We suggest that the source is a B-WD. Along with AR Sco, it being a B-WD constrains the death line model. B-WD hypothesis alleviates the necessity of an unusually high magnetic field hindering pair production for PSR J0901-4046 under the neutron star hypothesis. We argue that some rotation-powered pulsars with extreme properties may possibly be white dwarfs rather than neutron stars.

new.title: A new view of the cosmic-ray knee after LHAASO
new.summary: Recent LHAASO measurements offer a new view of the cosmic-ray knee by combining the all-particle spectrum and mean logarithmic mass with proton and light-component spectra across the PeV region. This contribution reviews these results and their implications for Galactic acceleration and transport. Approximately charge-ordered proton and helium knees coexist with different spectral evolution, while their turnover shapes constrain source populations and escape mechanisms. These measurements anchor an elemental ``ladder'' that, extended to heavier nuclei, will be crucial for establishing how far the Galactic component persists and where the Galactic--extragalactic transition takes place.

new.title: Can we constrain the binary neutron star merger time from kilonova light curves?
new.summary: The joint observation of gravitational waves (GWs) from a binary neutron star (BNS) merger (GW170817), together with a short Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB 170817A) and a kilonova (KN, AT2017gfo), marked the birth of multimessenger astronomy with GWs, and demonstrated the informative power of multimessenger observations. More BNS merger and KN detections are expected , thanks to the increasing sensitivity of GW detectors and the advent of new electromagnetic facilities such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. However, the association between a BNS merger and a KN might not be trivial: the detection of a KN might not coincide with the onset of the EM emission, making it difficult to define a temporal window to assess the coincidence with a GW event. In this work we investigate the possibility to constrain the BNS merger time from KN light curves, exploring different observing conditions and with focus on the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We used different KN models and different inference frameworks to simulate and fit KN light curves. We explored different cadences and wavelength coverages for observations, to investigate how the different observing conditions can affect the capability to recover the BNS merger time. The tests performed also include real data related to AT2017gfo, plus a few GRBs that have been associated to possible KN candidates. We find that, under realistic observing conditions with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the BNS merger time can be recovered with a precision of 5.5 days (90\% CI) with a best-case scenario with an accuracy of 0.18 day and a precision of 0.74 day (90 \% CI). Results can slightly improve (by $\sim$ 5 \%) if the source redshift is available. Upper limits near the merger time can also improve the results, reducing the width of the posterior by $\sim60$ \%. The BNS merger time estimate could also benefit from EM follow-up observations with other telescopes.

new.title: A Comprehensive X-ray Characterization of the Pulsar Wind Nebula CTB 87: Evidence for Reverse-Shock Interaction from Its X-ray and Broadband Emissions
new.summary: We present a comprehensive X-ray study of the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) CTB 87, utilizing new NuSTAR observations and archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data. Our joint analysis reveals that the PWN's X-ray spectrum exhibits significant curvature, well described by a broken or cutoff power law. The broken power-law fit yields photon indices $\Gamma_{1}=1.89\pm 0.05$ and $\Gamma_{2}=2.73 \pm 0.10$ below and above a break energy of $E_{\rm b}=5.12 \pm 0.26$ keV, respectively, while the cutoff power-law fit gives $\Gamma=1.23 \pm 0.10$ and $E_{\rm c} = 5.29 \pm 0.67$ keV. Spatially resolved spectroscopy confirms a previously observed radial softening of $\Gamma$, indicating significant synchrotron cooling as electrons move outward from the pulsar. We employed leptonic emission scenarios to model the broadband emission from CTB 87, focusing on the measured X-ray spectrum and the radial profiles. While an evolutionary one-zone model can explain the general features of the broadband spectral energy distribution (SED), its predictions do not fully reproduce the observed X-ray spectrum. Our multi-zone modeling demonstrates that the hard electron distribution required to explain the X-ray spectrum cannot account for the observed gamma-ray SED. This discrepancy suggests the presence of an additional electron population, possibly linked to the reverse shock interaction, and highlights CTB 87 as an evolved PWN whose broadband emission cannot be captured by these simple SED models. We discuss the potential origins for this second electron population and its implications for understanding the evolution of PWNe.

new.title: Probing the QPO and spectro-temporal evolution of MAXI J1750-327 with XPoSat during its first detected outburst : Constraints on black-hole mass and spin
new.summary: We present a comprehensive timing and broadband spectral study of the newly discovered black hole low-mass X-ray binary candidate MAXI J1750-327 during its August 2026 outburst, using 11 continuous observations obtained with the XSPECT instrument onboard XPoSat. During epochs 1-2, we detect prominent type C QPO exhibiting a systematic upward frequency drift, accompanied by a prominent low-frequency noise component, with a clear transition from type-C to type-B, with subsequent disappearance of QPOs after epoch 4. Broadband spectral modeling reveals that this timing transition is directly mirrored by a fundamental restructuring of the accretion geometry. The inner disk temperature abruptly increases before settling into a steady range, accompanied by a steep reduction in disk normalization across the transition from epoch 3 to 4. This behavior signifies an active dynamical inward migration of the thin accretion disk toward the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). The Comptonized flux declines sharply after the QPO turns off, suggesting a transition from a hard to soft state, through intermediate states. We also observed that the spectro-temporal correlations provide compelling physical support for the Lense-Thirring (LT) precession framework to be the origin of the type-C QPOs. Using a Bayesian framework, we constrain the black hole mass to be $M_{\rm BH}=7.92^{+6.19}_{-3.72} M_{\odot}$ and the dimensionless spin parameter to be $a_*=0.163^{+0.116}_{-0.056}$ by jointly modeling the observed type-C QPO frequencies with the global LT precession model and marginalizing over the uncertainties in distance, inclination, and diskbb normalization.

new.title: X-ray Comptonization in an Accreting Kerr Black Hole System with a Tilted Disc and Thermal Corona: A General-Relativistic Monte Carlo Simulation. II. Polarization Signatures
new.summary: Relativistic precession of the inner accretion flow is widely invoked to explain low-frequency QPOs, and the Relativistic Precession Model (RPM) predicts phase-dependent X-ray polarization. However, IXPE observations challenge simple precession and Comptonization models; for example: SwiftJ1727.8-1613 shows weak or undetected QPO-phase polarization modulation, while IGRJ17091-3624 shows a hard-state polarization degree (DOP) of ~9%, versus ~4% in other hard-state black hole binaries. In Paper I, we presented a general-relativistic Monte Carlo (GRMC) model of X-ray reprocessing in a misaligned, warped two-zone disc around a Kerr black hole with a hot, optically thin corona. We computed energy spectra, photon path-length and arrival-time distributions, and X-ray lags. Here, we extend the model to track photon polarization using Walker-Penrose parallel transport and polarized Compton and disc scattering. We calculate the energy-resolved degree and angle of polarization and their precession-phase modulation versus coronal optical depth, outer-disc albedo, photon-injection radius, and observer inclination. We find that gravitational light bending raises the mean DOP and enhances modulation, whereas coronal scattering and reflection from the misaligned outer disc lower the DOP and suppress modulation. The steady outer-disc polarization further dilutes the inner-flow signal. Their competition can produce weak, nearly unmodulated polarization or a high, strongly modulated signal. Strong scattering and reflection can explain SwiftJ1727.8-1613's weak modulation, while strong light bending and weak secondary scattering can explain IGRJ17091-3624's high DOP. Our results provide a framework for interpreting unusual X-ray polarization and testable predictions for constraining black hole parameters, coronal properties, and disc-warp geometry with IXPE, XPoSat, and eXTP.

new.title: Interpreting the $γ$-ray emission from Westerlund 1: hadronic or leptonic?
new.summary: High-energy $\gamma$-ray emission has been detected from several star clusters, indicating that these sources are sites of cosmic-ray acceleration. However, it is still unclear whether the $\gamma$-ray emission is of hadronic or leptonic origin. We present a comprehensive study of the $\gamma$-ray emission from Westerlund 1, under the assumption that high-energy particles are accelerated at the cluster WTS. We investigate both the hadronic and leptonic scenarios by fitting simultaneously the spectrum and morphology of the $\gamma$-ray emission. We numerically solve the transport equations for non-thermal protons and electrons for a given $K_\rm{ep}$ and derive their energy and spatial distributions. $\gamma$ rays are produced either by hadronic pp interactions of protons with the target gas or by inverse Compton scattering of relativistic electrons (both primary and secondary) with the ambient photon fields. We also calculate the synchrotron emission from these electrons. The predicted SEDs are compared with the $\gamma$-ray measurements by Fermi-LAT and HESS and with the X-ray upper limit derived by eROSITA. For reasonable model parameters, we find that in the case of Bohm diffusion, both the leptonic and hadronic scenarios can account for the observed multi-wavelength spectrum and $\gamma$-ray morphology. However, in the case of Kraichnan diffusion, better motivated in star clusters, only the hadronic scenario can explain the observations, while the leptonic scenario fails to reproduce the highest-energy $\gamma$-ray data points. For the leptonic scenario, the magnetic field immediately downstream of the shock can be constrained to be $\lesssim$ a few $\mu$G thanks to the eROSITA upper limit. On the other hand, in order to explain the $\gamma$-ray observations with hadronic emission alone, the gas density inside the bubble should be $\gtrsim 1.2 \, \rm{cm}^{-3}$.

new.title: Investigating a TeV-Halo Candidate around PSR J1928+1746 with HAWC
new.summary: We present an updated High-Altitude Water Cherenkov (HAWC) analysis of the crowded Galactic-plane area near PSR J1928+1746, which was previously linked to the extended source 3HWC J1928+178. With 2904 days of HAWC data, improved event reconstruction, and a multicomponent likelihood model that includes six TeV source components and Galactic diffuse emission, we describe the region using six components and find a distinct, moderately extended source close to PSR J1928+1746. This source, HAWC J1928+1750, is detected from about 2 TeV to above 100 TeV and is well-described by a log-parabola spectrum with normalization $K = 5.0 \times 10^{-15}$ TeV$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at 12 TeV, index $\alpha = 2.09$, curvature $\beta = 0.35$, and Gaussian extension $\sigma = 0.19^\circ$. Interpreting the emission using diffusion-halo templates under the assumption $B = 8 \mu\mathrm{G}$ yields the diffusion coefficient D(100 TeV) = $2.1 \times 10^{27}$ cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$, which is about 500 times smaller than typical interstellar diffusion values at similar energies. This suggests that particle transport around PSR J1928+1746 is strongly suppressed under the TeV-halo interpretation. The TeV spectrum is consistent with leptonic inverse-Compton emission originating from pulsar-injected electrons and positrons, which requires less than approximately 1% of the pulsar's characteristic spin-down energy. However, a hadronic contribution from the surrounding environment cannot be excluded.

new.title: Double-Shock Radiation in Supernova Wind Breakout and EP260321a
new.summary: We study the supernova (SN) shock breakout (SBO) from an optically thick stellar wind. The SN ejecta-wind interaction forms a forward shock (FS) plus reverse shock (RS) structure. The RS's internal energy and shock velocity are both a fraction $\mu\lesssim1/6$ of the FS's. The lower RS velocity makes it easier to build up local thermal equilibrium (LTE) and generate blackbody (BB) emission. In the same time a $\mu^{-1}\gtrsim6$ times larger non-BB emission may be produced by the likely non-LTE FS. We apply the theory to analyze the recent detected type Ic-BL SN2026gzf associated X-ray flash EP260321a, and find it is naturally accounted for by a SN wind breakout: the $\sim0.13$\,keV, thermal SBO emission can be produced by the RS during the interaction of a typical type Ic-BL SN ejecta ($E_k\sim10^{52}$erg and $M_e\sim1M_\odot$) and a stellar wind with a mass $M_w\sim10^{-4}M_\odot$ confined within a radius $r_w\sim10^{13}$cm; the X-ray rise time is mainly determined by the RS emission time, whereas the long duration and decrease time are due to the scatterings of SBO photons by a distant shell-like medium which has a large photosphere, $r_{ph}\sim10^{14}$\,cm; the early, within 30\,ks, optical emission can be naturally explained by the cooling emission of a shocked pure C/O envelope, since the observed SBO onset is delayed by $\gtrsim$ a few ks due to the large medium photosphere. BB+non-BB components from RS and FS, respectively, may be common in SN wind breakouts. SBO observations can be crucial in the study of progenitor stars by providing information for the ejecta from the SN explosion and the nearby wind from the pre-SN activities.

new.title: General Relativistic Simulations of the Nonlinear Evolution of r-modes in Rapidly Rotating Neutron Stars
new.summary: The r-modes in rotating neutron stars are a promising source of continuous gravitational waves, and may grow or be excited to amplitudes $\alpha\lesssim1$. We perform general relativistic simulations of nonlinear $l=|m|=2$ r-modes in a rapidly rotating neutron star with spin frequency $f_{spin}\approx792$ Hz, relaxing the Cowling and small-$\alpha$ approximations. The star is idealised as an unmagnetised, one-component, perfect fluid with a polytropic equation of state. The r-mode frequency is measured to be $f_{r-mode}=1014$ Hz for initial amplitude $\alpha_0=0.2$. The dimensionless frequency $\kappa\approx0.7197$ agrees with an estimate from linear perturbation theory to within 1.7%. $f_{r-mode}$ increases quadratically with amplitude, and $\kappa$ decreases by 3.4% across simulations where $\alpha_0$ is varied through the range $0.2\leq\alpha_0\leq1.2$. The gravitational wave strain calculated from the Newman-Penrose scalar implies $h_{r-mode}\approx9.7\times10^{-22}$ at $10$ kpc for $\alpha_0=0.2$, which agrees with Einstein's quadrupole formula to within 35%. We also report on nonlinear phenomena observed in our simulations, e.g. differential rotation, amplitude decay, and signatures of nonlinear mode coupling in the spacetime oscillations.

new.title: Lasting mEMRIs: Signatures of Multiple Black Hole Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals from AGN discs
new.summary: Encounters of stellar-mass black holes (sBH) in active galactic nuclei discs naturally form mean-motion resonances of sBH pairs. These mean-motion resonances can be broken close to the central supermassive black hole when gravitational-wave emission dominates over gas torques. We derive a simple condition that depends only on the sBH mass ratio and the resonance index for which a pair of sBH in a mean-motion resonance will remain intact and can be detectable as a multiple Extreme-Mass-Ratio-Inspirals (mEMRIs) in the LISA band. We present for the first time the gravitational-wave strain signatures of a pair of co-migrating sBH in mean-motion resonance, including additional gravitational-wave harmonics associated with orbital conjunctions of the individual EMRIs. The frequency evolution and the associated chirp mass is degenerate with isolated EMRIs of different masses. However, the mEMRI mass ratio is quantised by the resonance order and is larger than the true mass ratio. The degeneracy can be broken if the true sBH mass ratio can be inferred from individual strain amplitudes. We argue that mEMRIs should be common if disc driven EMRIs are to be detected by LISA, with $\sim 10$ mEMRIs per year in the local universe ($z \lesssim 0.2$), highlighting the need to model mEMRI systems in future LISA data analysis.

new.summary: Various models predict that gravitational-wave sources produce high-energy neutrinos. Among them are compact binary coalescences with at least one neutron star, but also core-collapse supernovae or accretion disk instabilities. Two different analyses are presented, combining data from the LIGO and Virgo gravitational-wave detectors with those from the ANTARES and ORCA neutrino telescopes observed during the third observing run of LIGO-Virgo. In the first analysis, selected high-energy neutrino candidates were used as triggers to search for gravitational-wave candidates. In the second analysis, a search was conducted for potential spatial and temporal coincidences between subthreshold high-energy neutrino candidate events and subthreshold gravitational-wave candidates emitted by compact binary coalescence systems. In both searches, no significant coincidences were found. Upper limits on the rate of sources emitting both high-energy neutrinos and gravitational waves are presented. In particular, with the joint search, a joint source rate density upper limit of $8.8\times10^2~\mathrm{ Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$ was found for a typical binary neutron star coalescence with a GW emitted energy of $10^{-1}~\rm M_\odot c^2$ and an isotropic energy emitted in neutrinos of $10^{51}~$erg.

new.title: Domain models of turbulent magnetic fields and the spectral shape of ensemble averaged axion-photon conversion
new.summary: Axion-like particles are light pseudoscalars that appear in many extensions of the Standard Model and are candidates for dark matter. Through their mixing with photons, they imprint energy dependent modulations on the spectra of astrophysical sources shining through magnetised media. When a distant source shines through the turbulent magnetic field of an intervening galaxy cluster, these modulations are stochastic. It has recently been shown that averaging over an ensemble of such sources instead produces a smooth absorption-like feature. In this work we derive the analytic form of this ensemble averaged signal, previously known only numerically. We further relate the index $a$ of the magnetic field energy spectrum to the index $\beta$ of the domain size distribution that simulations use to describe the turbulent field. For $1<a<2$ the two indices obey the simple analytic relation $\beta=3-a$. Any distribution with $\beta<1$ instead mimics the spectral index $a=2$, which the sharp domain walls impose. For Kolmogorov turbulence, relevant for galaxy clusters, the relation gives $\beta=4/3$.

new.title: PSR J0653+0443: An Eclipsing Millisecond Pulsar in an Extremely Eccentric Double Neutron Star System
new.summary: Double neutron star (DNS) systems emit gravitational waves (GW) as they orbit each other, with waveforms dependent on their orbital properties \cite{Poisson+ this http URL .....P}. The number of DNS systems surviving binary star evolution in the Milky Way and the distribution of their orbital parameters are fundamental questions for GW astronomy and binary evolution studies. Here, we report the discovery of a new Galactic field DNS system, PSR J0653+0443, comprising two ~1.4 $M_\odot$ components in an extremely eccentric orbit $e=0.992387$, $P_{\rm orb}=79.084$ d. Its unique orbital dynamics include a 46-minute transit from true anomaly $\theta=-90^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ and striking periastron relative motion (maximum acceleration 1.11~km~s$^{-2}$, peak speed 1.14$\times$10$^6$~m~s$^{-1}$. The pulsar undergoes an 85-second conjunction eclipse, indicating a nearly edge-on binary orbit. Short-term variations in the periastron advance induce significant pulse arrival time modulation spanning -2.91 to +2.49 ms --- at least an order of magnitude larger than that observed in any other DNS system. From this modulation, the non-relativistic periastron advance rate is constrained to $-1.5^{+0.9}_{-0.8}\times10^{-4}$ deg yr$^{-1}$. The extreme orbital eccentricity can only be attributed to a large kick velocity imparted during the iron-core collapse supernova of the progenitor of the second component. The predicted detection probability of such a PSR J0653+0443-like DNS system is $\lesssim 5 \times 10^{-3}$, implying that our discovery of this system challenges current understanding of binary evolution. This extraordinary DNS system emits periodic gravitational wave bursts, with the GW energy flux peaking at 0.357 mHz. This makes it an ideal target for the future LISAmax mission.

new.title: PBR sensitivity to boosted dark matter explanation for the KM3-230213A event
new.summary: POEMMA-Balloon with Radio (PBR) is a hybrid fluorescence and optical Cherenkov telescope that is a pathfinder instrument for a future Probe Of Extreme Multi-Messenger Astrophysics (POEMMA), together with a radio instrument, to be flown on a super pressure balloon in Spring 2028. One of its science objectives is follow up of astrophysical event alerts via signals of tau decays in the atmosphere, sourced by Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. The recent report of the KM3NeT Collaboration's muon event with $ E_{\mu}=120^{+110}_{-60}$ PeV sparked searches for beyond the standard model (BSM) physics explanations. Using a specific, boosted dark matter scenario which together with the KM3NeT observation, sets a scale for the fluence of boosted dark matter in this energy range, we assess the capabilities of PBR to constrain or discover such a source for a boosted dark matter energy spectrum above $\sim 10^8$ GeV. PBR has discovery potential for dark matter energies above $10^9$ GeV, and depending on BSM input parameters, to dark matter energies as low as $1.5\times 10^8$ GeV. While the analysis is focused on one BSM example, the methodology is applicable to any BSM physics that affects tau production in the Earth.

new.title: Extended vs. thin screen approximation in astrophysical settings
new.summary: Context: In the context of radio wave propagation through plasma concentrations and for gravitational lensing, the thin screen approximation often provides a suitable approximation for scattering and deflections caused by three-dimensional spatial structures. For scattering of electromagnetic waves from an extended medium, stochastic theories provide analytical bounds on ensemble averaged quantities, such as the scintillation index. If neither the conditions for a stochastic treatment nor the thin screen approximation are fulfilled, fully numerical methods are required. Aims: For an extended structure, the applicability of the thin screen approximation needs to be verified by comparing it with the fully three-dimensional scattering solution. We discuss various exact solutions to simple lensing geometries and provide numerical results for the propagation in the branched-flow regime, which is also of relevance in astrophysical applications. Methods: We transfer several analytical results obtained in quantum mechanical scattering theory to astrophysical settings and complement them with different numerical methods to quantify the deviations of thin screen theories from an extended medium results. Results: We provide the analytical results for spherical waves scattered by a point source and show the emergence of branchef flow in the intermediate regime between thin screen physics and stochastic media results.

new.title: Modeling MAD Sgr A* flares and their dependence on spin
new.summary: Aims: This study aims to place constraints on the spin of Sgr A* from recent flare observations. It models the flare kinematics in the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, evaluates their dependence on black hole spin, and assesses the correlation between the spin of the black hole and the astrometric observations in the Galactic center. Methods: Our study extends the work of Antonopoulou et al. 2025 to a range of black hole spins. A prominent flux eruption is identified in the simulation, and the evolution of the active region on the equatorial plane is tracked during the event. The flare model consists of a spherical hot spot ejected along the flux tube with a relativistic velocity. Results: In MAD simulations, the flux tube wraps around the jet funnel in the opposite direction to the black hole's spin. This dependence is imprinted on the flare trajectory and provides a strong correlation between the spin of the black and the flare kinematics. This analysis favors Kerr black holes, with a preference towards larger spin magnitude. Although prograde simulations show a consistent clockwise motion in the sky regardless of disk rotation, retrograde models require a clockwise accretion disk to account for the observations of July 22, 2018. Conclusions: A maximally rotating Kerr black hole is the most promising candidate for reproducing the observed flare trajectory in the vicinity of Sgr A*, illustrating a pass faction surpassing $90\%$ among the investigated flare models. In particular, determining spin orientation within this model is linked to the rotation of the accretion disk. Assuming a counterclockwise accretion disk, a prograde black hole with $a\geq1/2$ is able to reproduce the observed flare kinematics in the Galactic center. Conversely, assuming a clockwise rotation for the disk, the observations support both prograde and retrograde Kerr black holes with a large spin.

cross.title: Dyonic black holes supporting nearly-black self-gravitating thin shells
cross.summary: It has recently been revealed that dyonic black-hole spacetimes of a quasitopological non-linear electrodynamic field theory may be characterized by discrete radial regions with the property $dg_{tt}(r)/dr=0$ in which spherically symmetric massive {\it test} shells (Dyson shells with negligible self-gravity) can be supported in static equilibrium states. In the present paper we prove that the dyonic spacetimes of the non-linear electrodynamic field theory may also be characterized by the presence of radial regions with the dimensionless property $d[r\cdot g_{tt}(r)]/dr\to0^+$ in which massive {\it self-gravitating} thin shells that are on the verge of becoming black holes can be supported in static equilibrium states. Intriguingly, it is proved that the discrete radii of these self-gravitating nearly-black Dyson shells are universal in the sense that they are independent of the masses of the central supporting dyonic compact objects.

cross.title: Linear causality and stability constraints on relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics
cross.summary: In this work, we construct a theoretical framework for relativistic second-order magnetohydrodynamics based on entropy current analysis. The formalism consistently incorporates finite relaxation dynamics of the dissipative fluxes, providing a transient framework suitable for analyzing linear stability and short-wavelength causality. Utilizing linear mode analysis, we investigate the constraints imposed by causality and stability on this anisotropic system. By linearizing the theory around a homogeneous equilibrium state, we identify the magnetosonic, Alfvén, and charge-diffusion sectors, together with their coupling terms. For each sector, we derive asymptotic dispersion relations in both the long-wavelength (small-$k$) and short-wavelength (large-$k$) regimes, validating them against exact numerical roots. Our numerical analysis confirms the accuracy of these asymptotic solutions and uncovers a nontrivial angular dependence, especially near special propagation directions where the ordinary momentum expansion becomes less reliable. By evaluating the large-$k$ behavior of the propagating branches alongside the damping properties of non-hydrodynamic modes, we delineate the corresponding causality constraints. We find that the admissible linear causal domain is governed by the interplay between propagation direction, anisotropic transport coefficients, and relaxation times, with the resulting bounds being intrinsically mode-dependent. These findings provide a systematic theoretical basis for investigating linear stability and short-wavelength causality in relativistic magnetohydrodynamics beyond the first-order approximation.

cross.title: The renormalization-group running of neutrino mixing is undetectable
cross.summary: Quantum corrections make the parameters of a theory depend on an arbitrary renormalization scale, $\mu$. The renormalization-group (RG) running of neutrino masses and mixing is a standard tool to relate models defined at a high mass scale to measured values. A growing body of work holds that the running is also directly observable: a neutrino produced or detected at momentum transfer $Q$ would carry the mixing matrix evaluated at $\mu = Q$. Proposed signatures include flavor change at zero distance from the source, shifts in the measured CP-violation phase, and an anomalous flavor composition of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos. We show that this premise is incorrect. The mixing is a property of the neutrino itself, fixed by its self-energy on the mass shell, not by the process that produces or detects it. Setting $\mu = Q$ is legitimate, but then large logarithms in the self-energy undo the running; the premise incorrectly drops them. Hence, apart from small vertex and box corrections, every experiment measures the same mixing: the running is undetectable. We illustrate this in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, two seesaw models, and the Standard Model effective field theory. Independently, short-baseline data already limit the change of any one mixing angle between pion decay and detection at $Q$ of a few GeV to below $0.7^\circ$--$2.4^\circ$.

cross.title: NGC 3227 Blinks: An Extreme Changing-Look Event in a Seyfert Galaxy
cross.summary: We report a rapid optical changing-look event in the Seyfert galaxy NGC 3227: the optical continuum faded by more than 70% and broad H-beta emission nearly disappeared within weeks, before recovering within two months. Damped random walk simulations calibrated to the source's normal variability show that such a decline is unlikely for stochastic accretion fluctuations (p = 0.002). Simultaneous Swift monitoring reveals X-ray spectral hardening, pointing to enhanced line-of-sight absorption. During the dim state, reverberation mapping yields a persistent 6-8 day lag between the continuum and broad H-beta, showing that the broad-line region continued to reverberate and placing the obscurer interior to the broad-line region. Photoionization calculations require a fully ionized, Compton-thick column with N_H ~ 1.5 x 10^24 cm^-2 to reproduce the optical continuum suppression. Together, these observations demonstrate that compact, high-column-density obscurers interior to the broad-line region can produce extreme optical changing-look behavior on week timescales.

cross.title: How general relativity stacks up: Testing gravity by coherently combining gravitational-wave observations
cross.summary: A core mission of gravitational-wave astronomy is to test general relativity (GR) in the high-curvature, high-velocity regime. The field has already seen significant progress in this space, though a remaining challenge is how to combine data from a population of binary mergers. This can both boost the significance of potential GR violations, and develop a phenomenological picture of how deviations manifest in different mergers. We propose a framework to coherently combine gravitational-wave measurements to build a population-level test of physics beyond GR. We assume that deviations from GR are (i) strongest near the merger, (ii) vary smoothly with the total mass of the binary, and (iii) are most prominent in the $\ell=|m|=2$ mode. While these assumptions do not describe every possible deviation of GR, they provide us with a plausible starting point upon which a more general framework can be built. We apply our framework to 28 high signal-to-noise ratio binary black hole mergers from LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA's Fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog, finding no evidence for deviations from GR. Our framework allows one to show how deviations could vary as a function of total mass of the system. We argue that such a reconstruction can be used to convincingly distinguish between systematic waveform errors and genuine GR violations.

cross.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
cross.summary: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

cross.title: SpinOctopus: A Versatile, User-Friendly, and Extensible Public Code for General-Relativistic Ray-Tracing in axisymmetric spacetime
cross.summary: Relativistic ray-tracing algorithms serve as indispensable numerical tools for investigating gravitational theories and high-energy astrophysics. In this paper, we develop and release SpinOctopus, a versatile relativistic ray-tracing code tailored for arbitrary axisymmetric spacetimes, powered by a Fortran/Python hybrid architecture and OpenMP multi-threading acceleration. This numerical toolkit is capable of simulating timelike orbits and their corresponding light curves, null geodesics, as well as black hole images illuminated by a wide array of phenomenological sources, including geometrically thin and thick accretion disks, geometrically thin tilted disks, relativistic jets, spherically symmetric accretion flows, and point sources. To execute these tasks, users are solely required to specify the covariant metric tensor of the target spacetime and the simulation parameters within a dedicated configuration file. Benefiting from our customized adaptive step-size strategy for geodesic integration, SpinOctopus achieves an impressive processing efficiency of $\sim 800$ rays per second per thread on an Intel Core i7-14700 platform when simulating geometrically thick accretion disk images. Furthermore, the code provides transparent interfaces, allowing users to seamlessly modify the geometric and kinematic properties of the light sources. Additional capabilities, such as simulating Fe K${\alpha}$ fluorescent line profiles and geometrically thick tilted accretion disk images, will be introduced in future releases of the framework.

cross.title: Neutron Star-Main-Sequence Star Collision: Formation and Long-Term Evolution of Thorne-Żytkow Objects
cross.summary: Thorne-$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$ytkow objects (T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$Os) are stars containing a neutron-star (NS) or black-hole (BH) core embedded in a stellar envelope and powered primarily by mass accretion onto the core. Classical evolution models of T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$Os begin with an assumed equilibrium configuration and predict chemical anomalies in the stellar envelope resulting from nuclear burning in the vicinity of the NS core. Here we connect dynamical formation to long-term evolution by combining a three-dimensional simulation of a post-supernova collision between a $1.4M_\odot$ NS and a $10M_\odot$ main-sequence star with a subsequent stellar evolution calculation using MESA. The collision successfully produces a bound, quasi-spherical T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$O with the NS settled at the center of the stellar envelope. In contrast to the classical picture, the collision heats a substantial fraction of the star and leads to widespread nuclear burning during the subsequent thermal-relaxation phase. As the envelope becomes convective, material processed by the carbon-nitrogen cycle is transported to the surface, leaving a potentially observable chemical imprint of formation that persists after the star attains the standard accretion-supported T$\dot{\mathrm{Z}}$O structure. At the end of our simulation, the stellar luminosity greatly exceeds Eddington in the outer envelope, suggesting that significant mass ejection will occur, leaving behind an isolated NS or BH.

cross.title: Cosmic Ray Observations using Coincident Scintillator and Radio Signals with the Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON)
cross.summary: At energies above 100 PeV, coherent radio frequency (RF) emission across the 10 -- 1000 MHz band from cosmic particle-induced atmospheric showers becomes increasingly dominant, making radio detection a powerful probe at ultrahigh energies. The Beamforming Elevated Array for COsmic Neutrinos (BEACON) considers mountaintop phased radio arrays to monitor large areas at the horizon for upward-going geomagnetic emission in the 30 -- 80 MHz band produced as a consequence of Earth-skimming tau neutrinos. As part of ongoing efforts to measure the sensitivity of BEACON to such signals, the BEACON prototype identifies cosmic rays through the same emission mechanism. Prior to 2023, BEACON operated a four-antenna prototype, which successfully demonstrated identification of coherent and impulsive sources using a beamforming RF trigger. In 2023, we upgraded the instrument to six newly designed antennas and added an independent scintillator array to cross-validate radio-detectable cosmic rays. This work details the observation of 22 candidate cosmic-ray events in a scintillator-coincidence-triggered dataset using selection cuts based on expected radio characteristics. A simulation of the hybrid-instrument performance verifies this observation rate to within an order of magnitude. We estimate a background of 0.11 events by applying the selection cuts to synthetic datasets of uncorrelated radio-scintillator pairs that are randomly formed using fixed-rate software-triggered data. The reconstructed signal polarization angles are consistent with pure geomagnetic emission compared to various background classes.

cross.title: Rotation slows the instability of Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes
cross.summary: We present nonlinear 3+1 evolutions of rotating Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes. We construct stationary rotating drainhole solutions with a spectral solver up to an equatorial rotation velocity of 99% of the speed of light, validate the solver against published symmetric solutions, and correct an inconsistency in a published field equation. Perturbed only by truncation error, the evolutions show that rotation slows the radial instability of the static wormhole. Near 30% of the extremal angular momentum the unperturbed throat expands instead of collapsing, rather than the instability disappearing as second-order perturbation theory suggests. From 58% upward we find no evidence of instability over the evolved times; at the fastest spin this holds at three resolutions. Collapsing rotating throats emit an axisymmetric quadrupolar gravitational-wave burst whose energy grows with spin. Second-order perturbative initial data trigger the instability through their own truncation error, so they are unsuitable for stability studies.

cross.title: The diversity of late-time interaction in Type II supernovae
cross.summary: Studying core-collapse supernovae (SNe) beyond one year after explosion, when ejecta interaction with circumstellar material (CSM) progressively becomes the dominant power source, offers critical insights into the progenitor mass loss history. Using binary progenitors that underwent different levels of H-rich envelope stripping, we present radiative transfer calculations of the ejecta with CSM interaction in Type IIb, II-L and II-P SN scenarios covering epochs of 1.5 to 3-6yr, with a focus on the UV and optical properties. The impact of CSM interaction is evaluated for a cold-dense shell (CDS) of 0.1-2.0Msun (CDS velocity of ~5000-10000km/s) and shock powers of 1e39-1e41erg/s, producing a grid of about 200 models. We find that Lyalpha, MgII2800, and Halpha are typically the strongest individual lines, MgII2800 being the most constant relative to changes in time and in CDS mass. Lyalpha thrives at low CDS mass and is strongly attenuated otherwise. A large fraction of the emerging UV and optical flux is, however, influenced by a forest of Fe lines, which introduces strong optical depth effects. A myriad of other lines, generally forbidden, are predicted that each contain less than a percent of the total flux. N enrichment yield stronger N lines in the UV and optical. A subset of these models roughly match UV and optical observations of SNe 1993J, 1998S, 2013ej, and 2023ixf at 1.5-3yr, although matching the full range consistently is a challenge, in particular when dust must be invoked. Blue-red asymmetry of line profiles is typical of all lines in the UV, the more so at earlier times or higher CDS mass, even in the absence of dust. In our simulations, optical depth effects, associated with the gas or dust or both, quenches the emission of Lyalpha or [OIII]4958-5007A from regions within or below the CDS.

cross.title: Local tests of Schwarzschild-Bertotti-Robinson spacetime
cross.summary: We study weak field local tests of Schwarzschild-Bertotti-Robinson spacetime, which describes a static black hole embedded in an external magnetic field. Perihelion precession, deflection of light rays and time delay of radar echoes are the phenomena considered in this work to understand the possible effects of this external magnetic field on these observationally important tests. We not only derive weak field analytical results by employing appropriate methods, but also consider an exact approach to directly integrate the relevant geodesic equations, to both confirm those weak field analytical results and to obtain results beyond the weak field approximation.

repl.title: Modeling X-ray reflection spectra from disk returning radiation: Application to 4U 1630-47
repl.summary: Returning radiation is thought to play a key role in disk illumination of black-hole X-ray binaries in the high-soft state, yet it has not been fully incorporated into XSPEC reflection models. We present a new table model for reflection spectroscopy that self-consistently accounts for the returning radiation of the thermal component. To isolate this effect, we adopted the standard disk-corona configuration but disabled the corona, allowing the reflection spectrum to be produced solely by the self-irradiation of the disk. We applied our model to three NICER and NuSTAR simultaneous observations of the black-hole X-ray binary 4U 1630-47 during the soft state. The model fits the data well, suggesting that returning radiation from the disk could potentially explain the reflection features observed in this source. Our results suggest a rapidly spinning black hole ($a_* \sim 0.99$), a disk inclination of $i \sim 43^\circ-54^\circ$, a mass accretion rate of $\dot{M}_{\rm BH} \sim (0.13-0.25)\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$, and a source distance of $7.3-11.3 \,\rm{kpc}$, which is in broad agreement with previous studies.

repl.title: Jet Power Estimates of FSRQs PKS 1441+25 and Ton 599 from Broadband SED Modeling
repl.summary: Flat-Spectrum Radio Quasars (FSRQs) are among the most energetic and powerful active galactic nuclei, often exhibiting jet powers comparable to or exceeding the Eddington luminosity. In this work, we performed broadband spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling of two FSRQs PKS 1441+25 and Ton 599, using Swift-XRT/UVOT, NuSTAR, Fermi-LAT and VERITAS observations during 2015 and 2021, respectively. We considered four particle distribution models: a broken power law, a log-parabola, and two energy-dependent models in which either the diffusion or acceleration timescale depends on energy. Our results show that the jet power estimates derived from models with intrinsic curvature, such as the log-parabola and energy-dependent models, are of the same order as those obtained with a broken power-law distribution. This contrasts with the case of High Synchrotron Peaked Blazars (HBLs), where the power estimates can differ by nearly two orders of magnitude between models. We attribute this difference to the lower electron break energies typically observed in FSRQs. Consequently, our findings suggest that, unlike in HBLs, the estimated jet powers in FSRQs are relatively insensitive to the assumed particle energy distribution, reflecting the dominance of external Compton processes and weaker dependence on spectral curvature.

repl.title: Spectral energy-loss bump and $γ$-ray pulsar halos
repl.summary: The parent electron spectrum of $\gamma$-ray pulsar halos is determined by continuous injection and radiative energy losses, with the nonlinear nature of the latter expected to produce an age-dependent energy-loss bump in the halo spectrum. We demonstrate that the broadband $\gamma$-ray spectrum of the Geminga halo measured by Fermi-LAT and HAWC is consistent with this expectation. Its energy-loss bump appears in the GeV region and is primarily produced by electrons injected at the earliest stage. Therefore, fitting the data allows us to constrain parameters governing early electron injection, such as the pulsar braking index $n$ and initial spin period $P_0$. In addition, we show that another crucial condition for explaining the Geminga halo spectrum is a power-law index of the injection spectrum close to $1$, consistent with the X-ray observations of the Geminga pulsar wind nebula. Currently, no significant energy-loss bump has been detected in the spectrum of the Monogem halo; based on this, we also place preliminary constraints on $n$ and $P_0$ of Monogem. This work demonstrates that pulsar halo spectra can be used not only to constrain electron injection parameters, but also to provide independent estimates of certain intrinsic pulsar properties.

repl.title: Signatures of Lorentz violation in the bright ring for Sgr A* images from radiatively inefficient accretion flows
repl.summary: We have investigated the effects of Lorentz violation (LV) on the bright ring in Sgr A* images illuminated by the 230 GHz thermal synchrotron emission from radiatively inefficient accretion flows around a rotating LV black hole within the low-energy Hořava gravity framework. Our results reveal that the LV parameter reduces the bright ring diameter yet increases its width, luminosity, azimuthal asymmetry and orientation angle. A higher spin parameter strengthens the LV-induced effects on the bright ring properties. Increasing disk thickness reduces the ring diameter and enhances the LV parameter's effects on this diameter. The ring width shows no systematic dependence on the disk thickness. These quantities of the bright ring display similar trends against the black hole spin and the LV parameter for the rotating LV black hole. Using EHT observational data of Sgr A*, we find that, at fixed disk thickness, the parameter-space map illustrates that the bounded range of the LV parameter first broadens and then contracts with the growing black hole spin, and shifts toward smaller LV parameter values. In addition, the LV parameter narrows the bounded range of black hole spin: negative LV parameter values shift this range to a higher spin, while positive values shift it to a lower spin. Finally, we probe effects of the LV parameter on the peak position value and the width of the primary image and the $n=1$ photon ring for the rotating LV black hole. The peak positions and their widths nearly always decrease with the LV parameter. The peak position differences for various LV parameters are more pronounced for a purely Keplerian accretion flow. In addition, the primary image and the $n=1$ photon ring produced by purely radially free-falling flows are broader than their counterparts generated by purely Keplerian flows.

repl.title: Chana: A GPU-Accelerated Adaptive-Mesh Code for General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics with Multigroup M1 Neutrino Transport
repl.summary: This paper presents Chana, a GPU-accelerated, block-structured adaptive-mesh code for general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, multigroup M1 neutrino transport, and dynamical spacetime evolution using the Z4c formulation. Each physical module uses independently selected spatial discretizations and ghost-zone widths to balance accuracy and computational cost. Stiff radiation-matter interactions are treated implicitly, with Jacobians calculated analytically from the chain-rules. The code is written in C++20 and it uses MPI and Kokkos 5 for distributed-memory and performance-portable parallelism. The code is validated through a number of GRMHD, radiation transport, and dynamic spacetime tests. For a representative core-collapse supernova configuration with three neutrino species and 12 energy groups per species, the code achieves approximately $1.1 \times 10^6$ cell updates per GPU second on NVIDIA A100 GPUs using four-stage RK4 integration. Weak-scaling efficiency remains above 85\% up to 256 GPUs on Perlmutter.

repl.title: Ellis-Bronnikov Wormhole Shadows with Spherically Symmetric Accretion Flow
repl.summary: We investigate the observational differences between the Ellis--Bronnikov (EB) wormhole and the Schwarzschild black hole (BH) by performing general relativistic radiative transfer (GRRT) simulations. We consider a spherically symmetric steady-state accretion flow and perform GRRT simulations incorporating synchrotron emission. For both the EB wormhole and the Schwarzschild BH, the simulated images consist of a central shadow region and a bright photon ring. We find that both the shadow region and the photon ring of the EB wormhole are brighter than those of the Schwarzschild BH. These differences arise from the absence of an event horizon in the EB wormhole, allowing the emission from the accreting matter around and beyond the throat to contribute to the intensity. We also compare the simulated images with the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) observations of M87*. Although the total flux and the ring diameter are comparable with the EHT results, our models with the spherically symmetric accretion flow cannot reproduce the deep central brightness depression observed by the EHT, for both the EB wormhole and the Schwarzschild BH. This indicates that a non-spherical accretion flow is required for a detailed comparison with the EHT image.

repl.title: The role of major mergers in triggering super-Eddington accretion
repl.summary: JWST observations have opened a new era in the exploration of the high-redshift Universe, revealing black holes (BHs) with masses of several million solar masses already at $z>8$, challenging our understanding of their growth mechanisms. In this context, super-Eddington (SE) accretion has emerged as a promising solution and has been widely adopted in both numerical simulations and semi-analytical models. In this work, we investigate whether a major merger between two relatively low-mass halos ($M_{\rm halo}\sim10^9\,\mathrm{M_\odot}$) at high redshift can trigger episodes of sustained SE accretion, with particular focus on the role of BH feedback. We employ state-of-the-art, high-resolution cosmological zoom-in simulations of a major merger at $z\sim11$. We explore different prescriptions for BH seeding and feedback, including physically motivated radiative and kinetic models (winds and jets) across the three main accretion regimes: advection-dominated accretion flows (ADAF), radiatively efficient sub-Eddington accretion, and SE accretion. For the relatively low-mass halos studied here, our feedback prescription efficiently suppresses gas accretion, preventing substantial BH growth. We find that, although the merger drives gas inflows towards the central regions, this is not sufficient to trigger sustained SE accretion. Post-merger SE accretion episodes are observed only when BH feedback is entirely switched off. Amongst the feedback channels considered, kinetic feedback is the primary mechanism regulating BH growth. Moreover, the only significant SE accretion episodes occur immediately after BH seeding, while the merger itself does not produce a substantial enhancement of the accretion rate.

repl.title: Black hole populations and hierarchical growth across the AGN parameter space
repl.summary: Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have been proposed as efficient environments for the formation of binary black holes (BBHs). We present an updated semi-analytical framework for BBH formation and evolution in AGN disks, following the capture, migration, pair-up, gas-driven hardening, binary--single encounters, and merger of stellar-origin black holes. We systematically explore the dependence of the resulting BBH merger population on the main AGN parameters, namely the supermassive black hole mass $M_\bullet$, the Eddington ratio $\lambda_\bullet$, and the disk viscosity parameter $\alpha$, and construct an intrinsic BBH population by weighting the simulations according to observed low-redshift AGN properties. We find that AGN disks can produce repeated mergers and build a high-mass tail extending beyond the pair-instability mass gap and into the intermediate-mass range. Hierarchical growth is more efficient in lower-viscosity disks, with $\alpha=0.01$, while higher-viscosity disks suppress the formation of massive remnants. The merger efficiency generally increases with $\lambda_\bullet$, but its dependence on $M_\bullet$ is non-trivial. The AGN-assisted BBH population is characterized by increasingly unequal mass ratios at high primary mass, a correlation between primary mass and $|\chi_{\rm eff}|$, and an effective-spin distribution that depends strongly on the fraction of binaries born in prograde or retrograde configurations. We find that the AGN channel can reproduce systems broadly consistent with the massive BBH events GW190521 and GW231123. We test several variations of the physical model, including different formalisms for migration torques, gas hardening, and three-body encounters. The general properties of the population are robust across these variations, with the high-mass tail and spin signatures persisting in all cases except when gas hardening is switched off.

repl.title: SN Helios: A Multiply Imaged Type II Supernova Opening Time-Delay Cosmography beyond redshift of 3
repl.summary: We report the discovery and spectroscopic confirmation of SN Helios, a strongly lensed, multiply imaged Type II supernova (SN) at $z=3.34$ behind the galaxy cluster RXC J0018.5+1626. The transient was identified as a red F150W-dropout source (F277W = 26.1 mag) in JWST/NIRCam imaging taken on 2026 July 3 for the VENUS survey, with no counterpart in 2024 December imaging. Director's Discretionary Time observations on 2026 August 17 added second-epoch NIRCam imaging and a deep NIRSpec prism spectrum. The spectrum shows a strong, spectrally resolved H$\alpha$ emission line (FWHM $\approx 7900$ km/s) with a P-Cygni absorption blueshifted by 8800 km/s, together with corresponding H$\beta$ and He I $\lambda$10830 features, establishing a hydrogen-rich photosphere at $z=3.34$. Template fits classify SN Helios as a Type II SN, and light-curve comparisons with well-studied local SNe II yield a phase of $27.5\pm2.8$ rest-frame days past B-band maximum. Independent cluster lens models magnify the observed image by $\mu\approx 10$-20 and predict another image within $\simeq 2$-6 yr, offering a rare opportunity for a time-delay measurement of $H_{0}$ with a source at $z>3$. The host galaxy is undetected in deep rest-frame ultraviolet and optical imaging, in emission lines, and in ALMA 2 mm dust continuum, leaving a heavily obscured counterpart unlikely. Its de-lensed $M_{\rm UV}\gtrsim -13$ places it far below blank-field limits and adds support to an elevated core-collapse rate per unit star formation in ultra-faint galaxies. Without the multi-epoch data, SN Helios would masquerade as a convincing $z\approx 16$ Lyman-break galaxy, with galaxy-template fits strongly disfavoring any low-redshift solution even with multiple medium bands. Its spectrum thus provides an empirical SED template with which high-redshift searches can vet similar dropout candidates.
